title: Chill an orange LED in liquid nitrogen and its light turns yellow-green

cover.alt: A small LED held on wires above an insulated box, glowing bright yellow-green, next to a multimeter on a workbench.

body: An LED's colour is set by its semiconductor's **band gap**, the energy an electron gives up as a particle of light when it drops across that gap. The light comes out with a photon energy close to the gap, so a wider gap means bluer light. In semiconductors the gap usually shrinks as they warm up, because the atoms jiggle more and sit further apart. Dip an LED in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C and the gap widens enough to see: an orange LED shines yellow-green, then drifts back towards orange as it warms up again.

slides.alt: A lit LED on two wires hangs just above an insulated box of liquid nitrogen, next to a multimeter. It glows yellow-green, then over about twenty seconds its colour shifts through yellow to a warm amber.
slides.caption: Just lifted out of liquid nitrogen, an orange LED glows yellow-green. As it warms in the air, its light shifts to yellow and back towards orange.

slides.heading: Why cold makes the light bluer

steps.label: The atoms sit slightly closer together

slides.prompt: Red, green or blue: which colour of LED needs the widest band gap?
slides.detail: Of the three, blue light carries the most energy per photon, so it needs the widest gap. Red needs the narrowest.

slides.heading: Band gaps of some semiconductors
slides.note: At 302 K. A wider gap gives more energetic light: infrared, then red, through the rainbow to violet.

slides.question: What mainly decides the colour of the light an LED's chip gives off?
options: The band gap of its semiconductor
slides.explanation: LEDs emit photons with energies close to, and slightly larger than, the band gap of the semiconductor they are made of.
